title: Suspected Cauda Equina Syndrome: Identification and Urgent MRI Pathway

evidenceAudit.scope: Adult with suspected cauda equina syndrome (CES): red flag symptoms, emergency referral within 14 days of onset, emergency magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) within four hours of request, bladder scanning, computed tomography (CT) only if MRI is contraindicated, and surgical referral, using the GIRFT national pathway.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-18.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: Only the Getting It Right First Time (GIRFT) national pathway PDF was opened; page numbers were not reliable in the extracted text, so sections are cited by heading.

The pathway contains no analgesic, gabapentinoid, opioid or steroid advice and no doses; the only drugs named are for bowel care (senna and docusate) and sexual function (tadalafil or sildenafil), without doses.
No Saudi guideline was opened; NHS England timing statements (for example local MRI provision by June 2024) do not apply to Saudi hospitals.
Source pages were read through automated page extraction rather than page-by-page in the original documents, so each figure should be spot-checked against the source during clinical review.
The Saudi Food and Drug Authority (SFDA) drug registration site could not be opened from this environment, so registration of each medicine was not verified; check hospital formulary.

pathophysiology.summary: Compression of the cauda equina nerve roots can cause bladder, bowel, sexual and lower limb dysfunction. The GIRFT pathway states that MRI on its own cannot diagnose CES; diagnosis combines symptoms, signs and imaging. Bladder scan results should not be used in isolation as a discriminator for MRI or surgery. Incomplete CES (CES-I) and CES with painless urinary retention and overflow incontinence (CES-R) are treated differently for surgical timing.

symptoms: Difficulty initiating micturition or impaired sensation of urinary flow.
Altered perianal, perineal or genital sensation (S2 to S5).
Loss of sensation of rectal fullness.
Severe or progressive neurological deficit of both legs.
physicalSigns: Subjectively reported or objectively tested altered perianal sensation.
Bilateral leg weakness or sensory deficit.
Post-void residual volume on bladder scan.
redFlags: Recent onset (14 days or fewer) or deterioration of CES symptoms: emergency referral.
Painless urinary retention and overflow incontinence (CES-R).
precipitants: Lumbar disc herniation or other compressive lesion in the lumbar canal.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: MRI shows neural compression without CES; safety-net and refer to musculoskeletal triage.

differentials.condition: Other causes of bladder or neurological symptoms
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: No cause on MRI: consider alternative diagnoses and other specialties.

clinicalManagement.title: Identify red flag symptoms
actions: Ask about micturition, perineal and genital sensation, rectal fullness, sexual function and bilateral leg symptoms; record perianal sensation.
Do not use a bladder scan alone to exclude CES.

clinicalManagement.title: Make an emergency referral
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Immediately when onset is within 14 days or deterioration
actions: Refer to the nearest facility with emergency MRI; discuss the request with a senior decision maker.
Use urgent (two-week) musculoskeletal triage only for static symptoms beyond two weeks.

clinicalManagement.title: Emergency MRI
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Within four hours of the request
actions: MRI takes precedence over routine and elective cases.
If MRI is absolutely contraindicated, consider CT or CT myelogram.

clinicalManagement.title: Refer to the spinal surgical team when compression is confirmed
actions: CES-I: surgery as soon as possible (NCEPOD E1/E2) and document any delay.
CES-R: surgery at the surgeon's discretion but within 24 hours of MRI.

clinicalManagement.title: If MRI shows no compression
actions: Consider alternative diagnoses; safety-net and refer to musculoskeletal triage if neural compression explains sciatica.

medicationPlan.note: The GIRFT pathway gives no analgesic, gabapentinoid, opioid or steroid advice and no doses. Senna and docusate (bowel care) and tadalafil or sildenafil (sexual function) are named after surgery without doses. Follow the hospital analgesia and bowel care protocols.

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: Emergency referral to nearest facility with emergency MRI
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: CES symptoms or signs that started within the last 14 days, or deterioration.
Static CES symptoms for more than two weeks: musculoskeletal triage to be seen within two weeks.
As soon as possible and certainly within four hours of the request to radiology.

teaching.scope: Adult with suspected cauda equina syndrome (CES): red flag symptoms, emergency referral within 14 days of onset, emergency magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) within four hours of request, bladder scanning, computed tomography (CT) only if MRI is contraindicated, and surgical referral, using the GIRFT national pathway.
learningObjectives: Emergency referral when symptoms started within 14 days.
pitfalls: Using a bladder scan to decide against MRI.
Delaying MRI because the spinal team has not been called.
keyPoints: MRI alone does not diagnose CES.
Bladder scan is not a discriminator.

patientEducation: Explain that urgent scanning is needed and why.
Report any new loss of bladder, bowel or sensation.
lifestyleAndDiet: Bladder and bowel care advice after surgery.
mdtReferrals: Spinal surgery; radiology; urology and continence care; physiotherapy.
dischargeCriteria: MRI reviewed and surgical plan made, or alternative diagnosis with safety-net advice.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Spinal surgical follow-up; urinary function and catheter trial per pathway (pre-void scan over 500 mL or no void in six hours: long-term catheter; post-void under 100 mL: no catheter).
